problemText: A natural resource is classified as renewable if nature can supply a new amount of it within a person's lifetime. Which of the following is an example of a renewable resource?
choices: Coal buried deep underground that takes millions of years to form
Petroleum pumped from oil deposits that took hundreds of millions of years to create
Mineral ore containing copper that forms over timescales far longer than a human life
Wind energy that keeps blowing as long as the sun heats Earth's atmosphere
hints: The one-question test asks: can nature make more of it within a person's lifetime?
Look for a resource that nature keeps producing right now, not one that took geological ages to form.

problemText: A geothermal power plant uses heat energy from deep inside Earth to generate electricity for a city. Apply the one-question test to geothermal energy. Which statement correctly classifies this resource and gives the right reason?
choices: Geothermal energy is renewable because Earth continues to produce heat deep inside it at a pace that makes new heat available within a person's lifetime

Geothermal energy is nonrenewable because it comes from underground, just like coal and mineral ore, and resources found below Earth's surface cannot be replaced quickly enough to matter for human use
Geothermal energy is renewable because people can easily access it by drilling wells and the ease of extraction means the resource will never be depleted no matter how much we use
Geothermal energy is nonrenewable because it will eventually run out if we use too much of it over time, just like all other energy sources that humans depend on for power
hints: Remember that location underground does not decide the classification—only how fast nature resupplies it does.
The test asks whether nature can make more of this resource within a human lifetime, not whether the resource is easy to reach or might someday be used up.

problemText: A factory uses natural gas extracted from underground deposits to heat its buildings. The natural gas formed in Earth's rocks over hundreds of millions of years. Apply the one-question test to classify natural gas. Which statement is correct?
choices: Natural gas is renewable because it is found underground where nature is always at work creating new deposits in the rocks at the same speed we remove it
Natural gas is nonrenewable because nature cannot supply a new deposit of it within a person's lifetime
Natural gas is renewable because it comes from a gas form, not a solid like coal, and this physical state means it regenerates faster than solid resources can
Natural gas is nonrenewable because humans extract it from one place at a time, removing all the reserves from a single location before moving to drill another well elsewhere
hints: Ask yourself: can nature make a new supply of natural gas in the time a person lives?
The fact that it is underground or comes from far below tells you where it is found, but not whether it is renewable—only the timescale of resupply matters.

problemText: Two mining operations remove resources from the same geological area. Operation A removes iron ore, which took millions of years to form. Operation B harnesses geothermal energy from the heat in those same rocks. A student claims both operations must take the same amount of time to resupply because both work with resources from the same underground location. Explain why this claim is wrong, and classify each resource correctly.
choices: The claim is wrong because iron ore and geothermal energy come from different planets, so they cannot be compared at all in terms of how quickly nature resupplies them

The claim is wrong because one resource takes longer to form than the other, even though location does not decide the classification; iron ore is nonrenewable and geothermal energy is nonrenewable because both require millions of years to regenerate

The claim is wrong because location does not decide whether a resource is renewable or nonrenewable; iron ore is nonrenewable because it takes far longer than a lifetime to form, and geothermal energy is renewable because Earth keeps producing heat continuously
The claim is wrong because geothermal energy is much more useful than iron ore, so it must be classified differently based on how important the resource is to human needs
hints: The key warning from the lesson: where a resource is found does NOT decide its classification—only how long nature takes to resupply it does.
Test each resource separately using the one-question test: can nature supply more of it within a person's lifetime?

problemText: A student reads that coal and petroleum are both fossil fuels found underground and concludes that all fossil fuels must be nonrenewable. She then reasons that since fossil fuels are nonrenewable, any resource that is nonrenewable must also be a fossil fuel. Which part of her reasoning is correct, and which is incorrect?
choices: Both parts are correct because fossil fuels and nonrenewable resources refer to the same group of materials
The first part is correct, but the second part is incorrect because not all nonrenewable resources are fossil fuels—mineral ore is also nonrenewable but is not a fossil fuel
The first part is incorrect because fossil fuels can be renewable if they are found in certain locations
Both parts are incorrect because the classification of a resource depends on its location, not on how long nature takes to resupply it
hints: Recall the definition of fossil fuel from the lesson and consider whether it includes all nonrenewable resources.
Use the worked example of copper ore: it is nonrenewable but it is not a fossil fuel—this shows that 'nonrenewable' is a broader category than 'fossil fuel.'

problemText: An explorer discovers that a region contains sunlight, wind, coal deposits, and iron ore, all in the same geographic area. She also learns that deep geothermal energy is accessible there. A company wants to build an energy facility and must choose which resources to use based on how long nature takes to resupply them. Sort all five resources into renewable and nonrenewable groups using the one-question test, and then explain why a company trying to operate for the next hundred years might prefer to use one group over the other based on the principle of resource resupply.
choices: Renewable: sunlight, wind, geothermal energy; Nonrenewable: coal, iron ore. A company planning for a hundred years might prefer renewable resources because nature resupplies them within a person's lifetime, so the energy source will not run out during the company's operation

Renewable: coal, geothermal energy; Nonrenewable: sunlight, wind, iron ore. Location is the deciding factor in classification, so resources found underground last longer and are better for long-term company planning than surface resources

Renewable: sunlight, iron ore; Nonrenewable: wind, coal, geothermal energy. Solid materials are renewable because they can be mined and molded into new forms, while gases and energy forms are nonrenewable and deplete quickly

Renewable: geothermal energy only; Nonrenewable: all others. Only energy that comes from deep inside Earth is renewable because it is hidden and protected from human use, whereas all other resources are exposed and vulnerable to overuse
hints: Apply the one-question test to each resource separately: can nature supply a new amount within a person's lifetime?
Think about what 'renewable' means for a company's long-term planning: if nature keeps resupplying a resource fast enough, the company will not run out during its operation.

problemText: Natural resources are not spread evenly across Earth. What does this mean? Look for the choice that correctly defines resource distribution.
choices: Some places have large amounts of a resource while other places have very little or none of that same resource.
All places on Earth have exactly the same amount of every natural resource available to them for economic use.
Resources only exist in cities and towns, not in remote areas where population is sparse or development is limited.
A place that has one type of resource must also have all other types of resources in similar quantities and concentrations.
hints: Think about whether every place has the same amount of forests, minerals, and fertile soil.
Consider what 'uneven' or 'unequal' distribution means.

problemText: Region X has a concentrated deposit of valuable minerals underground and rock formations suitable for mining. Based only on this resource, which large-scale activity would this region best support? Use the lesson's examples of how resources match activities.
choices: Large-scale farming, because minerals can be processed and mixed into soil to replace nutrients lost over time.
Large-scale mining, because a mineral deposit is a concentrated amount of valuable mineral in one place.
Large-scale logging, because rock formations that contain minerals must be cleared away to access timber resources.
Large-scale fishing, because mineral deposits in underground rock attract groundwater to the region and support aquatic life.
hints: Remember: mining depends on having a concentrated amount of a mineral to dig out.
Look at which activity's need matches Region X's actual resource.

problemText: A student observes that Town A has wide, flat land with deep, fertile soil and steady rain, while Town B has thin, rocky soil in hilly terrain. The student concludes: 'Town A has better land than Town B.' Using the lesson's correction about comparing places with different resources, explain what is wrong with this conclusion.
choices: The student is correct; fertile land is objectively better than rocky land in all situations.
The student ranked one place above another because of which resources it has, but different resources simply suit different activities—neither is 'better.'
The student should have measured the land area of both towns before making a comparison.
The student forgot that Town B might have thick forest, which would make its land better after all.
hints: Recall the worked example about Sunfield and Pinehollow and how the correction addressed ranking.
Think about whether having one resource instead of another makes a place superior or just different.

problemText: Place 1 has thick forest but thin, rocky soil. Place 2 has fertile, flat, well-watered land but very few trees. A student claims: 'Place 1 cannot support any useful activity because it lacks fertile soil for farming.' Using the lesson's key ideas, identify the flaw in this reasoning and explain what activity Place 1's resources actually support.
choices: The flaw is that Place 1 is too far from Place 2 to share resources. Place 1's thin soil could still support farming if forests were removed.

The flaw is that missing the resource a particular activity needs does not mean a place has no resources at all. Place 1's thick forest supports large-scale logging, even though its soil does not suit farming.
The flaw is that the student should have checked whether Place 1 has minerals underground. Mineral deposits could make up for the lack of fertile soil.
The flaw is that thin, rocky soil is actually quite useful for farming because rocks protect plant roots. Place 1 can farm after all.
hints: Look for the choice that applies the lesson's key idea: 'A place missing one resource still has others.'
Think about what logging needs (trees) versus what farming needs (fertile soil and water).

problemText: Two regions are being evaluated for economic development. Region M has a rich mineral deposit but poor soil. Region N has excellent farming land but no known mineral deposits. A development planner writes: 'Region N is the better choice because it has fertile soil, and farming is more important to people than mining.' Using the lesson's ideas about resource distribution and activity, identify what the planner did wrong.
choices: The planner made a value judgment by ranking one region above another based on which resource it has, when in fact each region's resources suit a different activity, and neither resource is inherently 'better.'
The planner forgot that Region M might also have fertile soil hidden in another area that the geological survey did not yet uncover.
The planner should have counted how many people currently live in each region and whether they have the skills needed for that region's primary activity.
The planner incorrectly assumed that farming requires fertile soil; in reality, mining operations can also produce food through underground cultivation methods.
hints: Recall the worked example correction: 'Ranking one place above another because of which resource it has is not' what geography does.
Does the lesson say one type of resource is more important or 'better' than another?

problemText: A geographer studies four regions and their main activities: Region P (thick forest, logging); Region Q (fertile, flat, well-watered land, farming); Region R (thin soil, no forest, but mineral deposits, mining); Region S (unclear resources, struggling with all three activities). Based on the lesson's ideas about how resources shape activities, which statement best explains Region S's struggle and correctly identifies what Region S is likely missing?
choices: Region S must be a 'bad' place overall because it supports none of the three major activities as well as the others do, which shows that some places are naturally cursed with no useful resources whatsoever.

Region S likely lacks a concentrated amount of any one resource—it may have scattered trees, poor soil, and few minerals. Without large amounts of the specific resource an activity needs, that activity cannot operate at large scale.
Region S's people are not working hard enough to develop their economy; the lesson shows that resources are the only thing that matters, so Region S residents must have chosen not to succeed.

Region S probably has all three resources present in very small quantities spread across a wide area, which proves that uneven distribution of resources causes all regions with mixed resources to remain equally poor and underdeveloped.
hints: Think about what each activity requires: logging needs thick forest, farming needs fertile soil and water, mining needs a concentrated mineral deposit.
Consider what it means for a resource to be present 'in large amount' versus present but scattered or thin.

problemText: A student brings lunch in a metal container and washes it each evening so she can use the same container again tomorrow. What conservation practice is she using?
choices: Repair, because she is maintaining her container in working order by washing it regularly each time.
Reuse, because the same item is used again for its job instead of being thrown away.
Recycle, because she is cleaning the container to break it down and transform it into a different product.
Reduce, because she is washing rather than buying a new lunch container each day for her meals.
hints: The same container keeps doing the same job—lunch storage—day after day.
Think about whether the item is being broken down and remade, or just used again as-is.

problemText: A boy's shoes develop a hole in the sole. Instead of throwing them away, his parent glues the sole back together and he wears them for another six months. Which practice is this, and what does it accomplish?
choices: Reuse, because the shoes are being worn again in their original form rather than being discarded or transformed.
Recycle, because the parent is breaking down the shoe material and reforming it into a new product for use.
Repair, because fixing the broken part lets the same shoes keep doing their job without buying new ones yet.
Reduce, because fewer shoes are purchased overall when broken ones are fixed instead of being replaced with new pairs.
hints: The shoes were broken and then made to work again—what practice specifically fixes something that stopped working?
After the fix, the shoes do the same job for the same person, not a different job or a different product.

problemText: Two families need to carry their groceries home from the store. Family A uses plastic bags from the store one time and throws them away, then buys new bags the next week. Family B brought cloth bags from home, uses them for groceries, takes them home, and brings them back to the store again next week. Why does Family B's practice matter for conserving resources?
choices: They are reducing because they are making a choice to use fewer bags at the very start.
They are recycling because the bags are being remade into new materials each time.
They are reusing because the same bags do their job again instead of new ones being made each week.
They are repairing because they maintain their bags so they last longer before breaking.
hints: The bags still work perfectly—they were never broken and needed fixing.
The same set of bags keeps being used for the same job, week after week, rather than being thrown away.

problemText: A factory makes plastic toys. The factory changes its process so that each toy uses 20% less plastic from the very start, instead of using the normal amount and hoping people will recycle the toys later. Why is this change in practice a more powerful way to conserve the plastic resource than relying on recycling alone?
choices: Using less plastic from the start means fewer raw materials have to be drawn out and made into toys, so the resource lasts longer than if a normal amount were made and later recycled.
Reducing plastic in toys costs less money than setting up recycling programs, so factories will see profits increase and choose to conserve more over time.
Recycling plastic from old toys requires so much energy that it wastes more resources than simply reducing the amount made from the beginning of production.
Making toys with less plastic forces people to reuse their toys instead of throwing them away and buying new ones every few months.
hints: Think about the rate idea: conserving a resource means slowing how fast people draw from it. How does using less material from the start affect that rate?
Recycling does conserve, but it happens after the material has already been made into a toy. What happens if less material is needed for the toy in the first place?

problemText: A community collects old bicycles that no longer work and sends them to a repair shop. The shop fixes them and donates them to students who need transportation. Compare this to a scenario where the shop instead melts down the metal parts and remakes them into new bicycle frames. Which approach is an example of reuse, and why does it conserve the resource more effectively in this situation?
choices: Melting down and remaking is reuse because the metal material from old bicycles is being used to produce new bicycle frames instead of purchasing virgin metal from new mining operations.

Fixing and donating the old bicycles is reuse because the same bicycles do their job again rather than being thrown away or melted down, and each repair postpones the need for new bicycles longer than melting and remaking does.
Both are equally effective at conserving because both avoid throwing away the bicycles and both result in usable transportation for the community within a few months.
Fixing is reuse, but melting down and remaking into new frames is more effective because the metal gets transformed into a stronger, newer material with better performance for the students.
hints: Reuse means the same item keeps doing its job. Recycling means the material is broken down and remade into something new. Which is which?
Consider how long the resource lasts: does a bike that keeps working do more to slow down material use than bike metal that gets melted down and made into new frames?

problemText: A student notices that her school throws away cardboard boxes every week after deliveries arrive. She proposes three solutions: (1) the school could order supplies in smaller shipments so fewer boxes arrive in the first place; (2) the school could flatten the boxes and donate them to a local art program that uses them for projects; (3) the school could bundle the boxes, take them to a paper mill, and have them remade into new office paper for the school to buy back. Rank these three solutions from slowest to fastest at drawing down the cardboard resource over one year, and explain which practices they represent.
choices: Solution 2 (donate to art), then 1 (smaller shipments), then 3 (remake into new paper). Solution 2 is reuse, solution 1 is recycle, and solution 3 is reduce.
Solution 1 (smaller shipments), then 2 (donate to art), then 3 (remake into new paper). Solution 1 is reduce, solution 2 is reuse, and solution 3 is recycle.
Solution 1 (smaller shipments), then 2 (donate to art), then 3 (remake into new paper). Solution 1 is reduce, solution 3 is recycle, and solution 2 is reuse.
Solution 3 (remake into paper), then 1 (smaller shipments), then 2 (donate to art). Solution 1 is reuse, solution 2 is reduce, and solution 3 is recycle.
hints: Remember: reduce uses less from the very start, before anything is made or used. Reuse uses the same item again. Recycle breaks down used material and remakes it into something new. Which practice stops the need for new material earliest in the cycle?

Consider the rate of drawing resources: the fewer new boxes that arrive, the fewer new boxes ever need to be used, donated, or remade. Does cutting the supply at the source conserve faster than using what has already been made?

problemText: People in a cold climate with long winters wear clothing in layers. What does layering help the body do in a cold climate?
choices: It makes the body look bigger so other people notice the person.
It allows the person to add or remove pieces as the day gets warmer or cooler.
It traps warm air between the layers so body heat does not escape quickly.
It uses dark colors that absorb heat from the sun during the day.
hints: Think about how warm air moves between layers of clothing.
The lesson teaches that layering keeps heat from leaving the body.

problemText: A climate has heavy rain for many months each year, and rivers often flood low-lying areas and turn the ground into mud. Which transportation method would work best for people who need to travel during the rainy season in this climate?
choices: Bicycles and motorcycles, because they are light and do not need roads.
Heavy trucks with thick tires, because they can push through mud and floods without getting stuck or damaged.
Cars with sealed windows, because they keep people dry during floods and protect them from water damage.
Boats and raised walkways, because they let people move over water and mud instead of through it.
hints: Think about what happens to the ground during heavy rain and flooding.
The lesson teaches that transportation should work with water, not against it.

problemText: A climate stays hot and dry almost all year, with very little rain. People in this climate wear loose, lightweight, light-colored clothing. Why does this type of clothing fit this climate better than tight, heavy, dark-colored clothing would?
choices: Loose, lightweight, light-colored clothing lets air move against the skin and reflects sunlight, helping the body release heat instead of trapping it.
Tight, heavy, dark-colored clothing absorbs heat from the sun and traps warm air against the skin, making people feel hotter and more uncomfortable.
Loose, lightweight, light-colored clothing is easier to wash in dry climates where water is scarce and expensive to use.
Tight, heavy, dark-colored clothing prevents sweat from evaporating off the skin, which stops the body from cooling itself naturally.
hints: Think about how loose fabric lets air move and what happens when light colors are hit by sunshine.
The lesson explains that clothing should help the body release heat in a hot climate.

problemText: A region has long, cold, snowy winters and a short growing season when few crops can grow. A student claims that the best solution is to build greenhouses so people can grow fresh vegetables all year long, just like people do in warm climates with long growing seasons. What is wrong with this plan, and what adaptation would actually fit this climate better?
choices: Greenhouses are too expensive, so people should just move to warmer climates instead.

Greenhouses require constant energy to heat in a cold climate, which is costly and not how the climate itself works. Instead, people should store dried, preserved foods that last through the months when nothing grows.
Greenhouses work fine, but people in cold climates prefer to eat only frozen food because it tastes better.
Greenhouses let too much cold air inside during winter, so the extra fuel needed to keep them warm makes them impractical for long, harsh seasons.
hints: Think about what the toughest condition is in a long, cold, snowy climate and what food solution actually fits that condition.
The lesson teaches that an adaptation should match the climate's biggest problem, not fight against it.

problemText: A house is built with thick walls, small windows, and a steep roof in a climate with long, cold winters and heavy snowfall. A builder wants to use this same design for a new house in a climate that is hot and humid all year, with heavy rain and no winter season at all. Which statement best explains why this house design would NOT fit the hot, humid climate?
choices: Thick walls and small windows are too expensive to build in hot climates compared to thin walls with large windows.

Thick walls and small windows trap heat inside instead of letting it escape, making the house feel hot and uncomfortable. The same design that solves the cold-climate problem creates the opposite problem in a hot climate.
The steep roof is too steep for warm climates and will cause water to run off too quickly instead of keeping the house dry.
Small windows reduce air flow through the house, which prevents cool breezes from entering and makes it harder for the body to cool down naturally in hot weather.
hints: Think about what a thick-walled, small-windowed house does to heat and air movement.
The lesson teaches that the same adaptation can fail in a different climate because it solves a different problem.

problemText: A climate has a long, warm growing season with steady rain, so fresh fruits and vegetables grow for most of the year. Another climate is very cold and dry for eight months, with only a short period when crops can grow. A person claims that both climates should have the same food strategy: eating mainly fresh produce all year long. Using what you know about how food adapts to climate, explain why this claim is wrong for one of the climates, describe what food strategy would actually fit that climate, and explain why the claim works for the other climate.
choices: Fresh produce works everywhere because it is healthy. The cold, dry climate should grow hot peppers in winter, and the warm, wet climate should grow the same peppers all year.

The cold, dry climate cannot grow enough fresh food for eight months of the year, so it needs stored, dried, or preserved foods to last through the long season when little grows. The warm, wet climate has a long growing season with steady rain, so fresh foods can be grown and eaten across most months.
Both climates should use the same strategy because people need fresh food everywhere. The difference is only that cold climates need to refrigerate produce, and warm climates do not.

The warm, wet climate is too humid for fresh produce to stay fresh, so it should only eat dried food. The cold, dry climate has a short growing season but can use stored food just like the warm climate does.
hints: Think about the growing season in each climate and what happens when little or nothing can grow for months.
The lesson teaches that food adapts to what the climate allows to grow and to how long storage must last.
